claims.value: GM Hillinger commanded side B's brigade, left behind by Rosenberg. Without precise knowledge of the events at Caldiero, he wanted to do his utmost to ease the main army's fight: he left 2 companies at S. Anna and advanced to the heights of Fojano, without the caution that the presence of considerable enemy detachments in front and on his right flank urgently demanded (Angeli). He refused a summons to surrender (Angeli: made on 1 November; Koch: cut off and summoned, unable to believe himself completely abandoned, he disdainfully sent the envoy back), awaited the attack on 2 November standing fast and repulsed it. Rosenberg's order to fall back on Ala arrived shortly afterwards, when it could no longer be carried out (Angeli); Koch says Hillinger received at nine in the morning the order to withdraw in all haste to Ala by Santa Anna and the val Freddo to join Hiller, and formed a screen of about a thousand men of the Banat to mask his retreat. He refused a second summons; his troops fought on until 4 in the afternoon, and when 400 men covered the field and ammunition began to run short he accepted the capitulation offered him for the third time (Angeli).
claims.rationale: Side B's decisions at the engagement as both accounts give them, read from the page images. Angeli says Hillinger's conduct was not above reproach tactically; that is his judgment (claim bodart-winner). English renderings (ours): Angeli, 'without precise knowledge of the events at Caldiero, he wanted to do his utmost to ease the main army's fight'; as in claim angeli-side-b for the 2 companies and the heights of Fojano; 'notwithstanding this most dangerous situation GM Hillinger thought of no retreat, but firmly refused the summons to surrender made still on 1 November and on 2 November awaited the attack standing fast'; 'he did indeed repulse it bloodily, but when shortly afterwards the order came from FML Prince Rosenberg to go back to Ala and either join the army by forced marches through the Val Sugana at Bassano or join FML Hiller, carrying it out was already impossible. (75.)'; Koch, as in claim koch-side-a for the summons; 'his situation was becoming more and more critical when he received at nine in the morning the order to withdraw in all haste to Ala by Santa Anna and the val Freddo in order to join General Hiller's corps'; as in claim koch-side-b for the screen; Angeli, as in claim angeli-side-a for the second summons; 'until 4 in the afternoon the imperial troops fought the hopeless fight undaunted'; 'only when 400 men covered the field and ammunition began to run short did GM Hillinger accept the capitulation offered him for the third time; 1800 men laid down their arms and became prisoners of war, the officers released on their word of honour'.

claims.value: Bodart records a victory of side A (French) under Marshal Masséna over side B (Austrian) under GM Hillinger. Both other accounts end the action with Hillinger's capitulation (Koch; Angeli: he accepted the capitulation offered for the third time). Angeli judges that, though Hillinger's conduct was not above all reproach tactically, he gloriously preserved the honour of arms and considerably hindered the pursuit of the imperial army at its most dangerous stage; the sentence before his section on the action says Masséna's intention of following the Austrian army was held up for hours by an incident lying quite apart from the great events.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome (side A won), read from Bodart's entry, with the other accounts' ending (page images, except Angeli's sentences on Masséna's intention and the delay, OCR). No source read gives a different result. Angeli's verdict on Hillinger and on the delay is his own judgment, not a measured effect; his section 'Gefecht bei Fojano' follows the sentence on the incident directly. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Koch, 'then Hillinger capitulated'; Angeli, as in claim side-b-command for the capitulation; 'even if GM Hillinger's conduct in tactical respects was not above all reproach, the merit remains his beyond dispute of having gloriously preserved the honour of arms and considerably hindered the pursuit of the imperial army in its most dangerous stage. (76.)'; 'unable to hinder his march, he wanted to lose no moment in at least getting on his heels again and hampering his already extremely difficult movement as far as he could' (OCR); 'to the advantage of the imperial army, however, this intention too was held up for hours by an' (p. 148, OCR) 'incident lying quite apart from the great events' (p. 149, OCR); 'action at Fojano' (p. 149).

claims.value: Side A's information before the action was poor. Koch calls the reports of side A's patrols, pushed out along the whole line in the night the Austrian columns withdrew, exaggerated; among the movements that followed from them Hillinger was marching on Veronetta at the head of 7,000 men and Rosenberg was threatening side A's left. Koch asks whether the Archduke's movements were meant to mask his retreat, make a diversion beyond the Adige, seize Veronetta, isolate Seras to crush him or force Masséna to recross the river: Masséna's uncertainty was complete, he had no news of the Grande Armée on the Danube, and prudence led him to concentrate his army and reinforce the garrison of Veronetta. Angeli says Serras, misled by Hillinger's advance, had reported a movement of Rosenberg's against Veronetta. The care with which the Archduke surrounded his departure from Caldiero fully achieved its aim, and Masséna was told of it only in the forenoon (Angeli); Koch says he had notice of the Austrian movements too late to put serious obstacles in their way. Seras was informed of Hillinger's movement and sent troops after him (Koch). The firing in his rear and the report of the repulsed attack disturbed Masséna (Angeli; Koch: the retreat of the 22nd and the firing in the rear gave him a moment's anxiety), and he then sent Solignac. The screen of Banat men rejoined the 2 companies at Santa Anna unknown to side A (Koch).
claims.rationale: Side A's information as both accounts give it (page images, except Koch's sentences on Masséna's dispositions and on when he had notice of the Austrian movements, and Angeli's on Serras's report, on the Archduke's precautions and on when Masséna was told, all OCR; the hour, date and ordinal in Angeli's sentence are not restated). claims.value: Side A attacked. In Koch, Charpentier had Hillinger attacked at once by the 22nd, which was thrown back; Solignac, sent to envelop Hillinger, attacked when the new summons was refused, supported by dragoons and cuirassiers, and Hillinger capitulated. In Angeli, Hillinger awaited the attack on 2 November standing fast and repulsed it, and after he refused a second summons 8 battalions and 14 squadrons advanced to the attack from all sides. Side B's earlier advance to the heights of Fojano (Angeli) and on Ca Albertini (Koch) was the demonstration against Veronetta it had been ordered to make.
claims.rationale: Both accounts have side A attack Hillinger's brigade, and Angeli says the brigade awaited the attack standing fast, so the code is A_attacked. Side B's advance was a demonstration ordered from above, and no passage read has it attack side A's positions; in Koch the 22nd attacked it and was thrown back onto the château's breaches. Side A's attacks were ordered by Charpentier, chief of the general staff, and by Masséna through Solignac (claim side-a-command), so the posture is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): Koch, as in claims koch-side-a and side-a-command; Angeli, as in claims side-b-command and angeli-side-a; the demonstration as in claims angeli-side-b and koch-side-b.

claims.value: The passages read place side B on the heights of Fojano (Angeli) and at Ca Albertini (Koch), with 2 companies at S. Anna, and side A's men in the château San Felice, Seras's detachment sent by Parona and San Rocco and Solignac's column sent into the val Pantena; they name no works from which side B fought. The one work named is the château San Felice: Koch says the 22nd, too inferior in number, was thrown back onto its breaches, and Verdier gathered the men he met in the château and moved against the enemy; he does not say either side fought from it.
claims.rationale: Code none_named: no passage read has either side fight from works. The castle's breaches are named only as the place onto which side A's beaten regiment was thrown back, and the castle as the place where Verdier gathered men before moving against the enemy, so they are recorded here and not coded as side A fighting from works. none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed. English renderings (ours): Angeli, as in claim angeli-side-b for the heights of Fojano and S. Anna; Koch, as in claims koch-side-b and side-a-command for Ca Albertini, the 22nd and the castle; as in claim koch-side-a for the 22nd, Verdier, Seras and Solignac.

open_questions: Deferred: Koch's p. 108 before the Hillinger passage (the defence of Vicenza; not transcribed) and his pp. 106-107 beyond the sentences cited, read in the OCR, which follow side A's pursuit of the Austrian rear guard; any French report of the action, such as Solignac's or Charpentier's, which the passages read do not cite; the sources Angeli cites (note 75: Major Geppert's report from Arzignano and Hillinger's own report from Treviso, Kriegsarchiv F. A. XI; note 76: the journal of the imperial army in Italy, F. A. XIII, the Oesterreichische militärische Zeitschrift and Koch's volume V; the notes read in the OCR). Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated in values: the hour and date at which Masséna was told of the Austrian departure and the ordinal of the stage the Austrian main body had reached by then; the date, hour and number of battalions in Rosenberg's order to Hillinger; the number of battalions with which Angeli's OCR has Hillinger mask Rosenberg's march to Velo.

Most consequential gap: side B's strength and loss. Angeli gives 7 battalions and 2 squadrons with no number of men, Koch 8 battalions and 4 squadrons, Bodart about 4,000 men, and side A's patrol reports 7,000; Angeli and Bodart give 1800 (1,800) prisoners and Koch 5,000, more than Bodart's strength. Hillinger's own report (Treviso, Kriegsarchiv F. A. XI, cited in Angeli's note 75, read in the OCR) or a French return of the prisoners could close it. Side A's total, Bodart's about 12,000, is not in the passages read either.

Disputes recorded in the claims: side B's prisoners (Koch 5,000, with Hillinger and 70 officers sent back on parole; Angeli 1800, with the officers released on their word; Bodart 1,800); side B's strength (Koch 8 battalions and 4 squadrons; Angeli 7 and 2; Bodart about 4,000). The accounts agree on the result, on a first attack by side A that side B threw back, and on a body of side B escaping to S. Anna (Angeli: a battalion of the 2nd Banal Grenz regiment; Koch: about a thousand men of the Banat).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his losses for both sides equal Angeli's figures, and his two strengths are not in the passages read); Koch (a French history written from Masséna's papers); Angeli (an Austrian history from the Kriegsarchiv; by his notes, read in the OCR, written from Geppert's and Hillinger's reports and the army's journal; note 76 also cites a page of Koch's volume V, page number read in the OCR, so he is not wholly independent of Koch for this action).
